title_en: Supreme People's Court Releases Five Typical Cases
full_text_en:
Supreme People's Court Publishes Five Typical Cases

I. Defendant Fan Aidong, Wang Shenghua, Cai Jun — Environmental Pollution Case

(1) Basic Facts

In late July 2012, Shandong Xingfu New Materials Co., Ltd. needed to dispose of sulfuryl chloride, a dangerous chemical byproduct. Xing Bin (separately prosecuted), Assistant General Manager of the company, after consulting with General Manager Liu Genxian (separately prosecuted), arranged with defendant Fan Aidong to pay Fan Aidong RMB 300 per ton for disposal. On July 25, 2012, Fan Aidong directed defendants Wang Shenghua and Cai Jun to drive a tanker truck to Shandong Xingfu New Materials Co., Ltd., where they collected 35 tons of sulfuryl chloride, receiving RMB 10,500. At approximately 2:00 a.m. on July 27, Fan Aidong, Wang Shenghua, and Cai Jun drove the tanker truck to the Xiaoqing River Bridge at Tangkou Village, Huagou Town, Gaoqing County, Shandong Province, and dumped the 35 tons of sulfuryl chloride into the Xiaoqing River. The toxic gas clouds produced by the reaction of sulfuryl chloride with water drifted to Hantao Village, Jiaotou Town, Zouping County, Shandong Province, waking villagers from their sleep, causing respiratory damage to over a hundred villagers, and significant property losses including crops and seedlings. Villager Han Xuefang (victim, female, died at age 42), who had pre-existing conditions such as dilated cardiomyopathy, inhaled acidic irritant gases, leading to tracheal and pulmonary congestion and edema, directly increasing cardiac and respiratory load, resulting in acute respiratory and circulatory failure and death. On July 28, Wang Shenghua was arrested; Fan Aidong and Cai Jun surrendered.

(2) Judgment

The Zibo City People's Procuratorate of Shandong Province indicted defendants Fan Aidong, Wang Shenghua, and Cai Jun for endangering public security by dangerous means before the Zibo Intermediate People's Court. After trial, the Zibo Intermediate People's Court held that the defendants Fan Aidong, Wang Shenghua, and Cai Jun, in violation of state regulations, dumped the corrosive and irritating chemical sulfuryl chloride into the river, seriously polluting the environment and causing particularly serious consequences, including one death and substantial property damage. Their conduct constituted the crime of environmental pollution. The facts charged by the prosecutorial authority were established, but the charge was incorrect. In accordance with the Criminal Law of the PRC and the relevant provisions of the Supreme People's Court and Supreme People's Procuratorate's Interpretation on Several Issues Concerning the Application of Law in Handling Criminal Cases of Environmental Pollution, the court found defendant Fan Aidong guilty of environmental pollution and sentenced him to six years and six months' imprisonment and a fine of RMB 150,000; defendant Wang Shenghua guilty of environmental pollution and sentenced him to six years' imprisonment and a fine of RMB 100,000; defendant Cai Jun guilty of environmental pollution and sentenced him to five years and six months' imprisonment and a fine of RMB 100,000. After the judgment was pronounced, all defendants accepted the verdict and did not appeal.

(3) Typical Significance

Since the Supreme People's Court and Supreme People's Procuratorate's Interpretation on Several Issues Concerning the Application of Law in Handling Criminal Cases of Environmental Pollution took effect on June 19, 2013, it has resolved the previous difficulties in environmental pollution cases regarding "evidence collection," "identification," and "determination." Courts nationwide have intensified efforts to combat environmental pollution crimes, concluding a batch of such cases. According to incomplete statistics, as of December last year, courts nationwide had concluded over 100 criminal cases in which convictions were entered for the crime of environmental pollution, the crime of illegally disposing of imported solid waste, or the crime of dereliction of duty in environmental supervision. Among these, over 80 criminal cases resulted in convictions for environmental pollution, with this case being a typical example. The trial of this case strictly delineated the distinction between the crime of environmental pollution and the crime of endangering public security by dangerous means, and fully demonstrated and utilized the functional role of the people's courts in lawfully punishing environmental pollution crimes and promoting ecological civilization construction and healthy economic and social development.

II. Qihoo 360 Technology Co., Ltd., Beijing Qizhi Technology Co., Ltd. v. Shenzhen Tencent Computer Systems Co., Ltd., Tencent Technology (Shenzhen) Co., Ltd. — Unfair Competition Dispute

(1) Basic Facts

Tencent Company and Tencent Computer Company are internet companies providing comprehensive internet services. Tencent QQ instant messaging software and the Tencent QQ instant messaging system are their core products and services. On October 29, 2010, Tencent Company and others discovered that Qihoo 360 Technology Co., Ltd. (hereinafter "Qihoo") was providing downloads of "360 QQ Protector" software developed by Beijing Qizhi Technology Co., Ltd. (hereinafter "Qizhi") through the website www.360.cn, and was promoting it through various channels. Tencent Company and others alleged that this software directly targeted Tencent QQ software, using false propaganda to encourage and induce users to delete value-added service plug-ins of Tencent QQ software and block its client advertisements, while embedding Qihoo's own products and services into Tencent QQ software's interface, thereby promoting and marketing its own products. Tencent Company and others claimed that these actions by Qihoo and others not only destroyed their lawful business model, severely undermining the integrity and security of their products and services, but also seriously damaged their commercial reputation and product goodwill. They filed a lawsuit with the Guangdong High People's Court, arguing that Qihoo's conduct violated generally recognized commercial ethics and constituted unfair competition, and requested the court to order the two defendants to: 1. immediately cease the alleged unfair competition practices, including but not limited to developing, distributing, and disseminating "360 QQ Protector" and related software, cease the existing functions of the distributed and disseminated "360 QQ Protector" software, and cease acts of denigrating the plaintiffs and their products and services; 2. publish apologies on relevant websites and newspapers for three consecutive months to apologize to the plaintiffs and eliminate the adverse effects; 3. jointly and severally compensate the plaintiffs for economic losses of RMB 125,000,000; 4. bear the reasonable expenses incurred by the plaintiffs in enforcing their rights and all litigation costs.

(2) Judgment

After first instance by the Guangdong High People's Court and second instance by the Supreme People's Court, the courts held: In a market economy, the market plays a decisive role in resource allocation, and free competition can ensure optimal allocation of market resources. However, a market economy also requires fair, lawful, and orderly competition. Business operators in market transactions shall follow the principles of voluntariness, equality, fairness, honesty, and credibility, and abide by generally recognized commercial ethics. Acts that violate the Anti-Unfair Competition Law, harm the lawful rights and interests of other business operators, or disrupt the socio-economic order constitute unfair competition. In this case, to achieve their commercial objectives, Qihoo and others induced and provided tools to actively assist users in altering the operational mode of QQ software, simultaneously guiding users to install 360 Security Guard to replace QQ Software Security Center, thereby undermining the security of QQ software-related services and posing a significant threat to QQ software as a whole. This reduced Tencent's economic income and value-added service transaction opportunities, violating the principle of honesty, credibility, and generally recognized commercial ethics. Qihoo and others, without factual basis, claimed that QQ software would forcibly inspect users' computer hard drive privacy files, used their own standards to evaluate QQ software, and asserted that QQ had severe health problems, causing user panic and negative evaluations of QQ software and its services. Such commentary exceeded the scope of legitimate commercial evaluation and commentary, crossing legal boundaries. In operating QQ Protector, Qihoo and others embedded their own products and services into the QQ software interface, replacing part of QQ's functions. Their fundamental purpose was to leverage QQ's large user base, promote 360 Security Guard through disparaging QQ software and its services, thereby increasing their own market transaction opportunities and gaining competitive advantage. This conduct essentially constituted an improper use of another's market achievements to seek business opportunities and gain competitive advantage, violating the principles of honesty, credibility, and fair competition, and constituting unfair competition. The judgment ordered: 1. Qihoo and Qizhi jointly and severally compensate Tencent Company and Tencent Computer Company for economic losses and reasonable rights enforcement costs totaling RMB 5,000,000. 2. Qihoo and Qizhi publish an apology on the homepage prominent positions of their websites (www.360.cn, www.360.com) for 15 consecutive days, on the prominent homepage positions of Sina (www.sina.com), Sohu (www.sohu.com), and NetEase (www.163.com) for 7 consecutive days, and on the front page prominent positions of Legal Daily and China Intellectual Property News for 7 consecutive days, to apologize to Tencent Company and Tencent Computer Company and eliminate adverse effects.

(3) Typical Significance

This case was publicly heard by the Supreme People's Court on its Open Day in 2013 and was the first second-instance case handled by the Supreme People's Court involving unfair competition in the internet sector. The parties involved were both major enterprises in the internet-related fields, and the outcome attracted widespread attention from industry, academia, and others. Through this case, the Supreme People's Court clarified and established relevant market competition rules, marking a milestone for orderly competition among internet enterprises and promoting optimal allocation of market resources. After the public pronouncement of the judgment, relevant news media websites provided extensive coverage, and netizens highly praised the decision.

III. Abbott Trading (Shanghai) Co., Ltd. v. Taizhou Huangyan Yilong Plastic Co., Ltd. and Beijing Yiyangjie Trading Co., Ltd. — Pre-litigation Injunction to Cease Patent Infringement and Patent Infringement Dispute

(1) Basic Facts

Abbott Trading Company is the licensee of design patent No. ZL200730158176.0, titled "Container" (the patent-in-suit), and has obtained authorization from the patentee to apply for pre-litigation preservation measures and file lawsuits in its own name against infringers. Yilong Company, without authorization, manufactured, sold, and offered for sale sealable plastic containers (hereinafter "accused infringing products") of models "YL-650A," "YL-750A," and "YL-1000A" that infringed the patent-in-suit. Yiyangjie Company, without authorization, sold the accused infringing products. Abbott Trading Company applied to the Beijing No. 3 Intermediate People's Court for a pre-litigation injunction to cease the accused infringement and provided a cash guarantee.

(2) Judgment

The Beijing No. 3 Intermediate People's Court held: The accused infringing products are milk powder cans. Yilong Company and Yiyangjie Company primarily wholesale the accused infringing products to milk powder manufacturers, who then sell these products together with milk powder to end users. Each sales link likely constitutes infringement of the patent-in-suit. Each additional sales link expands the loss, increases the number of infringers, and raises Abbott Trading Company's enforcement costs and difficulties. Additionally, the patent-in-suit is a design patent for a container, valid only for ten years. Container designs undergo rapid updates. The continued infringement would significantly affect Abbott Trading Company's exercise of its patent rights. Therefore, if Yilong Company and Yiyangjie Company were not ordered to immediately cease the accused infringement, it would cause irreparable harm to Abbott Trading Company's lawful rights and interests. Accordingly, the court ruled that Yilong Company immediately cease manufacturing, selling, and offering for sale products infringing the patent-in-suit; Yiyangjie Company immediately cease selling products infringing the patent-in-suit.

After the ruling, through multiple communications and coordination with both parties, the court elucidated legal principles, prompting the respondents to shift from initially refusing to accept litigation documents to voluntarily ceasing the accused infringement, ultimately facilitating a settlement agreement and resolving the dispute through mediation.

(3) Typical Significance

This case is a typical example of the people's courts safeguarding food safety and protecting intellectual property rights accurately, timely, and effectively. First, in terms of social impact, food safety, especially milk powder safety, is a major public concern. Abbott milk powder is a world-renowned brand. The outcome of this case promptly curbed the proliferation of counterfeit milk powder cans, tackling counterfeit milk powder at its source, demonstrating the courts' commitment to people's welfare and food safety. Second, regarding enhanced IP protection, the court considered specific factors such as sales channels, enforcement costs, and the term of protection, accurately determined the "irreparable harm" requirement for behavioral preservation, swiftly issued a pre-litigation behavioral preservation ruling, and protected the parties' rights accurately and timely. Third, to ensure the practical effect of the pre-litigation behavioral preservation, the court actively urged the respondents to comply with the preservation ruling, ultimately facilitating a settlement agreement, effectively protecting the applicant's rights, and fully realizing the social effect of promoting mediation through behavioral preservation. This case was the first pre-litigation behavioral preservation ruling involving patent rights issued by a Beijing court under the amended Civil Procedure Law, demonstrating the courts' proactive response to social judicial needs and their practical efforts to strengthen judicial protection of IP rights.

IV. Tang Lan v. Cheng Yongli — House Sale Contract Dispute

(1) Basic Facts

On November 7, 2000, the Jiulongpo District Land and Housing Ownership Registration Center of Chongqing received documents concerning the sale of Tang Lan's house, including a "House Sale Contract" and "Application for Registration of Real Estate Transaction Contract," with Tang Lan as the seller and Cheng Yongli as the buyer. These documents bore a private seal reading "Tang Lan," and some were signed with the name "Tang Lan." Based on these documents, the Registration Center transferred the ownership of the house registered under Tang Lan's name to Cheng Yongli. On April 17, 2003, Tang Lan filed an administrative lawsuit with the court, claiming she never signed a house sale contract with Cheng Yongli. The Chongqing No. 1 Intermediate People's Court dismissed Tang Lan's lawsuit in second instance on the ground of lack of standing, stating in its reasoning that Tang Lan and Cheng Yongli had sealed and signed a standard-form real estate sale contract, and after review by the registration authority, the ownership transfer was approved. In March 2007, Tang Lan filed a civil lawsuit with the Jiulongpo District People's Court of Chongqing, seeking a declaration that the house sale contract was void and an order for Cheng Yongli to return the disputed house to Tang Lan. During the trial, the court found that the signature "Tang Lan" had been written by Cheng Yongli's husband, and the private seal reading "Tang Lan" could not be proven to belong to Tang Lan. The case went through first instance, second instance, and retrial by the Chongqing High People's Court, which debated whether the contract was valid or void. The Chongqing High People's Court's retrial judgment held the contract valid and accordingly dismissed Tang Lan's claims. Tang Lan, dissatisfied, petitioned the procuratorial authority. On May 16, 2012, the Supreme People's Procuratorate filed a protest with the Supreme People's Court.

(2) Judgment

In the retrial, the Supreme People's Court held that the contract issue was not about validity or invalidity, but whether the contract was established. Where there is a dispute between the parties over whether a contractual relationship exists, the party claiming the existence of the contractual relationship bears the burden of proof. Since the signature "Tang Lan" was confirmed not to have been written by Tang Lan herself, and Cheng Yongli could not prove that the private seal reading "Tang Lan" belonged to Tang Lan and was affixed by her, Cheng Yongli should bear the litigation consequences of failing to meet the burden of proof. The facts found in the administrative ruling only proved the legality of the housing authority's administrative action, not the establishment of a civil act. Moreover, multiple pieces of evidence demonstrated that Tang Lan did not sign the "Real Estate Sale Contract," and no house sale contractual relationship existed between Tang Lan and Cheng Yongli regarding the disputed house. Accordingly, the Supreme People's Court ordered Cheng Yongli to return the house to Tang Lan.

(3) Typical Significance

During the trial of this case, for the first time, the Supreme People's Procuratorate accepted cross-examination by the parties in court, which is of great significance for enriching and developing China's civil protest procedures. As to the form of contract validity in this case, the parties debated between validity and invalidity, and the lower courts also ruled based on that dichotomy. However, upon trial, it was discovered that the contract only involved the question of whether it was established. Based on this, the court correctly applied the rules of burden of proof regarding contract formation, reasonably allocating the burden of proof, thereby protecting the parties' substantive rights. This case provides guidance on the application of the burden of proof in civil judgments.

V. Wei Zhuofu v. Zhang Baofeng, Zhang Zezheng, Li Yuming — Enforcement of Notarized Creditor's Rights Document Case

(1) Basic Facts

Wei Zhuofu and Zhang Baofeng were neighbors. In 2011, Zhang Baofeng borrowed RMB 41,000,000 from Wei Zhuofu for business funding, with a term of one year. Li Yuming, a friend of Zhang Baofeng, voluntarily assumed joint and several guaranty liability for the debt, and Zhang Baofeng's son, Zhang Zezheng, voluntarily provided his house as mortgage collateral for the loan. On December 8, 2011, Wei Zhuofu entered into a "Loan Contract" with Zhang Baofeng, Zhang Zezheng, and Li Yuming, which was notarized with enforceable effect by the Beijing CITIC Notary Office. After the repayment period expired, Zhang Baofeng failed to repay the principal. On September 18, 2013, Wei Zhuofu applied to the Beijing CITIC Notary Office for an "Enforcement Certificate," which confirmed that Zhang Baofeng should repay Wei Zhuofu the principal of RMB 41,000,000 plus corresponding interest and liquidated damages, that Li Yuming bore joint and several guaranty liability, and that Zhang Zezheng bore mortgage guaranty liability.

(2) Enforcement Status

On September 27, 2013, Wei Zhuofu applied to the Beijing Chaoyang District People's Court for compulsory enforcement. After receiving the case, the enforcement judge contacted the judgment debtor to urge voluntary performance of the repayment obligation, but the judgment debtor refused to perform. Subsequently, the enforcement judge lawfully sealed up four properties and three vehicles owned by the three judgment debtors. On December 30, 2013, the enforcement judge again contacted Zhang Baofeng by phone to urge performance. Zhang Baofeng not only showed no willingness to perform voluntarily but also acted arrogantly and verbally threatened the enforcement judge.

On January 9, 2014, six enforcement officers, including the enforcement judge, together with media representatives, arrived at Zhang Zezheng's house, located in Chaoyang District, Beijing, covering over 900 square meters, to carry out enforcement. At the scene, there were four people employed by the judgment debtor: a nanny, a driver, a cook, and a tenant. After the enforcement judge presented identification, these individuals still obstructed the enforcement. After gaining control of the scene, the enforcement judge lawfully posted an auction notice on the door of the house and served a summons and a order restricting high consumption on Zhang Baofeng, restricting him from high-consumption activities such as flying and staying at high-end hotels. During enforcement, the enforcement judge also seized a Bentley car key belonging to the judgment debtor on the spot.

The next day, Zhang Baofeng proactively called the enforcement judge, admitted his mistake, and expressed willingness to actively perform the repayment obligation. On January 22, 2014, Wei Zhuofu submitted an enforcement settlement agreement to the court, and the case was successfully concluded.

(3) Typical Significance

This case is a typical example of a judgment debtor who has the ability to perform but refuses to perform legal obligations. The three judgment debtors in this case lived in affluence, owned several properties, lived in a luxury home worth nearly RMB 60 million, owned multiple luxury cars including a Bentley and a BMW, yet refused to repay their debt. After the court initiated enforcement, Zhang Baofeng remained defiant, refused to perform, and even verbally threatened the enforcement judge, resisting enforcement. This is a typical case of a judgment debtor lacking good faith.

The court in this case issued a high consumption restriction order against the judgment debtor, prohibiting him from traveling by air or train soft sleeper, restricting his access to loans or credit card applications, barring him from serving as a legal representative, director, supervisor, senior manager, etc., of an enterprise, and imposing credit sanctions on him within the social credit system. This created an enforcement deterrence effect whereby the debtor was restricted everywhere due to dishonesty, and his living space was compressed to the maximum extent. It was only after suffering such credit sanctions that the judgment debtor in this case proactively contacted the applying creditor and reached a settlement agreement. This fully demonstrates that credit sanctions are an effective enforcement deterrence mechanism. Meanwhile, during the enforcement process of this case, the enforcement court recorded the entire process of compulsory enforcement truthfully through media exposure, which not only deepened society's understanding of enforcement work but also deterred other judgment debtors and obligors, enabling people to intuitively perceive the serious consequences of refusing to perform judgments. The process of enforcement in this case illustrates that, in addition to guiding the formation of a social atmosphere of honesty and trustworthiness and promoting the construction of a social credit system, the media also has the function of facilitating obligors' fulfillment of their obligations, thereby reducing enforcement costs and enhancing enforcement efficiency.
